clue.text: Decline of Eton agreed in going mixed

indicators.note: letters that go mixed are jumbled, so the three words before this are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that Eton's standards slipped once it agreed to admit girls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going mixed' signals the anagram of ETON AGREED IN; 'of' is a link word. The surface leans on Eton, the famous English boys' school, turning co-educational.
explanation.definitionFit: A decline is a falling-off in quality, which is what a process of deterioration describes.

clue.text: Holding equipment I left, sat up at work surface

indicators.note: one piece holding another wraps round it, so the reversed word encloses the trimmed one
in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: to sit for a portrait is to pose, so sat means posed

indicators.note: left here means departed, so the I goes out of the word for equipment

parts.note: kit is gear or equipment

explanation.surface: Someone who has sat up at a desk, holding the gear they kept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the word for sat into DESOP; 'left' drops I from the kit to leave KT, which 'Holding' puts inside. 'at' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: The top of a desk is a flat surface for working at, and the word also names a computer that sits on one.

clue.text: Film farewell speech to carpenter?

parts.note: what you say on parting, a word of farewell
Chips is the traditional nickname for a carpenter, so a farewell addressed to one goes to Mr Chips

explanation.surface: A question asking what you would say when bidding farewell to a carpenter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chips' is a long-standing British nickname for a carpenter, from the wood chips of the trade. The title is a 1939 film from James Hilton's novel about a schoolmaster.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of a classic British film about a retiring schoolmaster, so it is an example of a film.

clue.text: Given lowest place in navy, princess flipped

indicators.note: flipped means turned over, so the whole combined piece is read backwards from the bottom
the princess sits inside the abbreviation for the navy

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy
Ida is the princess in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera Princess Ida

explanation.surface: A princess in the navy, demoted to the bottom rank and turned over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' gives RIDAN, which 'flipped' reverses whole. 'Given' is a link word. Princess Ida is the heroine of a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera.
explanation.definitionFit: In astronomy and in figurative use, the nadir is the lowest point, the bottom of anything.

clue.text: Strange: Times leader said to be lacking authority

parts.note: rum is old British slang for strange or odd
the newspaper speaks of itself as ours, so The Times gives our
ED, short for editor, is the leader of a newspaper's staff

explanation.surface: A newspaper's chief is reported to be oddly lacking in authority.
explanation.walkthrough: The Times would call its own editor 'our ED', which is the playful reading of 'Times leader said'; 'said to be' are link words. RUM is British slang for odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Something only rumoured is unconfirmed hearsay, a report without the backing of any authority.

clue.text: Gull is to change course of hearing

indicators.note: something given 'of hearing' is the word as heard, so a word that sounds the same is entered

parts.note: to change course is to turn

explanation.surface: A seabird that changes direction when it hears something.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the word for changing course and the seabird's name sound identical.
explanation.definitionFit: Loosely a gull, this is a slender seabird of the same family, so the clue uses the related bird as a stand-in.

clue.text: Vow formerly broken by monkish historian, I held

indicators.note: a word broken by another is split open with that other placed inside it

parts.note: once means at a former time, formerly

indicators.note: I is held inside the historian's name

parts.note: the Venerable Bede was an Anglo-Saxon monk who wrote a history of the English church

explanation.surface: A monk who wrote history breaks an old vow while he holds the narrator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held' makes BEDIE; 'broken by' splits the word for formerly after its O. The Venerable Bede, an eighth-century Northumbrian monk, is the crossword's usual historian.
explanation.definitionFit: Obedience is one of the three monastic vows, alongside poverty and chastity.

clue.text: What protects against infection? One's not affected by the answer

parts.note: someone immune is not affected by something
a response is an answer

explanation.surface: A question about what fends off disease, then a remark about someone unmoved by a reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' and 'by' are link words: one is unaffected, and an answer follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The body's defensive reaction to a pathogen is what guards it against infection.

clue.text: Contribute money, as Greeks did to Troy?

definitions.meaning: to put money into a venture expecting a return
an old sense meaning to lay siege to or surround a city with troops

explanation.surface: Putting money in, compared with the Greek siege of Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the archaic military one, to besiege.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both putting capital into something and, in old usage, besieging a town.

clue.text: Rate son unfeeling

parts.note: a cold person is unfeeling

explanation.surface: A judgement that a son is heartless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rate' here is the old verb meaning to berate, not to assess or value.
explanation.definitionFit: To rate someone, in an old sense, is to rebuke them angrily, which is to tell them off.

clue.text: Book named awfully likely victim

parts.note: Mark is a book of the New Testament

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters of the word beside it are scrambled

explanation.surface: A book whose title is terribly named, picking out its probable victim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully' scrambles the clue word to EDMAN. 'Book' is so often a Bible book in cryptics that a Gospel name is worth trying first.
explanation.definitionFit: A person singled out as a target for attack or revenge is someone likely to become a victim.

clue.text: Emperor is closing university after capital outflow

indicators.note: the river comes first and the rest follows after it

parts.note: the Tiber flows out through Rome, the capital

indicators.note: is closes round, enclosing, the letter for university

explanation.surface: An emperor shutting a university after money has drained from the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital outflow' looks like finance, but it is the river flowing through Rome. 'closing' puts U inside IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiberius succeeded Augustus as the second Roman emperor.

clue.text: Work out the form

definitions.meaning: to calculate or reason something out

explanation.surface: Instructions to exercise and get in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work out' and 'form' suggest the gym; 'the' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to calculate or reckon; as a noun it means a shape or outline.

clue.text: Group of sisters pleased I cooked

indicators.note: cooked suggests something altered or fiddled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted with a meal they prepared for a family of sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' rearranges PLEASED and I.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Pleiades were the seven daughters of Atlas, later a star cluster.

clue.text: In a small stream, nothing's holding wild minute, creature

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'In a small stream, nothing's holding wild minute, creature': A + RILL holding MAD, then O, builds the answer, leaving 'minute' with no job; the scan is blank and a search found nothing.
annotationWithheld.clue: In a small stream, nothing's holding wild minute, creature

clue.text: Turn up wearing green

parts.note: to be in clothes is to be wearing them
vert is the heraldic word for green

explanation.surface: Someone turns up dressed in green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn up' looks like arriving, but means to turn upside down. VERT is green in heraldry.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn something upside down is to invert it.

clue.text: City around lake needs sound boat

parts.note: CA, short for circa, means around

indicators.note: sound here means as spoken, so a word that is said like it is entered

parts.note: a cutter is a small boat

explanation.surface: A city by a lake that needs a seaworthy vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective (seaworthy) but signals a homophone: CUTTER said in a non-rhotic British accent. 'needs' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the older English name of Kolkata, a major Indian city.

clue.text: Be mean as old bag, concealing millions

indicators.note: concealing means hiding inside, so the abbreviation for millions sits within the bag

parts.note: a scrip is an archaic word for a small bag or satchel

explanation.surface: Being stingy like an old purse that hides millions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old bag' sounds insulting but is the archaic satchel SCRIP. 'as' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrimp is to economise stingily, to be mean with money.

clue.text: Glaswegian, say, shortly to employ another city's dialect

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: someone from Glasgow is an example of a Scot
to employ something is to use it

explanation.surface: A Glaswegian briefly adopting the accent of another city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' cuts SCOT to SCO. Scouse is the Liverpool dialect; Glasgow and Liverpool are both British port cities.
explanation.definitionFit: Scouse is the accent and dialect of Liverpool, which is a city other than Glasgow.

clue.text: Squint over consecutive letters in window

indicators.note: one word put over another covers it, so the squint wraps round the letters

parts.note: a cast in the eye is a squint
em and en are the spelt-out names of M and N, which follow one another in the alphabet

explanation.surface: Peering over a sequence of letters seen through a window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consecutive letters' are M and N written as their names, EM and EN; 'over' puts CAST round them.
explanation.definitionFit: A casement is a window hinged at the side so it opens like a door.

clue.text: Working outside is not exciting

indicators.note: working suggests the letters being worked over and rearranged

explanation.surface: Doing a job out of doors is dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working' rearranges OUTSIDE; 'is' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tedious is boring and dull, the opposite of exciting.

clue.text: Love to cross old area of land in leather

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, written O
a cross is drawn as X
a hide is an old English measure of land, enough to support a family

explanation.surface: A lover crossing an ancient tract of land clad in leather.
explanation.walkthrough: A HIDE was a medieval English unit of land; 'to' and 'in' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Leather made from the skin of an ox is ox hide.

clue.text: Fought being abandoned in a heap?

definitions.meaning: to scrap is to brawl, so this means brawled
thrown on the scrap heap, discarded as useless

explanation.surface: A tussle that left something abandoned in a pile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being' is a link word; the question mark marks the playful scrap-heap sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both brawled, from scrap as a fight, and discarded as junk.

clue.text: Discharged a ball, keeping in front of The Times cannon

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Discharged a ball, keeping in front of The Times cannon': A + RED holding C (front of cannon) gives the answer, but 'The Times' has no job, so the clue as held looks garbled; the scan is blank.

clue.text: In pain, old man's no good

parts.note: pa is a familiar word for one's father, one's old man

explanation.surface: A father in pain because he is useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' and the possessive are link words; PA is Dad, and NG the common shorthand for no good.
explanation.definitionFit: A pang is a sudden sharp pain.

clue.text: Beggar easily influenced by drink

indicators.note: by means next to, so the drink stands beside the word for easily influenced

parts.note: to sup is to drink
a pliant person is easily swayed

explanation.surface: A beggar easily won over by the offer of a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' only says the two pieces sit side by side; the clue gives them in the opposite order to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A suppliant is someone who humbly begs or entreats.

clue.text: Wide river is argument against journey

parts.note: a con is an argument against, as in pros and cons
a go can be a trip or turn, a journey

explanation.surface: Someone argues against making a trip across a broad river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Congo is one of Africa's great rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Congo is a vast African river, among the widest and deepest in the world.

clue.text: Opera lovers' wild party, with Elizabeth on piano

indicators.note: on means placed next to, so the other pieces are joined to the musical abbreviation

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
an orgy is a wild party of lovers
with means and
Bess is a pet name for Elizabeth

explanation.surface: An operatic scene of a lovers' orgy with Elizabeth at the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' joins P with the rest. P stands for piano in music; BESS is a short form of Elizabeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Gershwin's work about the lovers in Catfish Row is a famous American opera.
